etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English flowe, from the verb (see below). The psychology sense “state of focus” was coined by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi in 1975.

definitions.definition: Movement in people or things characterized with a continuous motion, involving either a non solid mass or a multitude.
The movement of a real or figurative fluid.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter IV, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: Mr. Cooke at once began a tirade against the residents of Asquith for permitting a sandy and generally disgraceful condition of the roads. So roundly did he vituperate the inn management in particular, and with such a loud flow of words, that I trembled lest he should be heard on the veranda.

definitions.definition: (mathematics) A formalization of the idea of the motion of particles in a fluid, as a group action of the real numbers on a set.
The rising movement of the tide.
Smoothness or continuity.
The amount of a fluid that moves or the rate of fluid movement.
A flow pipe, carrying liquid away from a boiler or other central plant (compare with return pipe which returns fluid to central plant).
(psychology) A mental state characterized by concentration, focus and enjoyment of a given task.

quote.citation: 2014 January 14, Alex Lockwood, “How to achieve a state of flow when running”, in The Guardian‎[1]:
quote.text: The point about flow is that it is enjoyable. As research has shown "the more often athletes experienced flow, the happier they were." But the second is that entering flow actually improves performance.

definitions.definition: The emission of blood during menstruation.
(rap music slang) The ability to skilfully rap along to a beat.

quote.citation: 2003, “In da Club”, in Get Rich or Die Tryin', performed by 50 Cent:
quote.text: Now shawty said she feelin' my style, she feelin' my flow  […]  / My flow, my show brought me the dough / That bought me all my fancy things

definitions.definition: (software) The sequence of steps taken in a piece of software to perform some action.

quote.citation: 2015, Dan, “Best practices for tracking progress through a sign up flow”, in snowplow-user mailing list‎[2]:
quote.text: I'm setting up event tracking for a pretty standard, multi-step signup flow, and I'm wondering [...]

etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English flowen, from Old English flōwan (“to flow”), from Proto-West Germanic *flōan, from Proto-Germanic *flōaną (“to flow”), from Proto-Indo-European *plōw-, lengthened o-grade form of *plew- (“to fly, flow, run”).

Cognate with Saterland Frisian flouje (“to flow”), West Frisian floeie (“to flow”), Dutch vloeien (“to flow”), Norwegian flo (“to flow”). Compare also English float. Not cognate with Latin fluō despite similarity.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To move as a fluid from one position to another.

quote.citation: 2008, BioWare, Mass Effect (Science Fiction), Redwood City: Electronic Arts, →ISBN, →OCLC, PC:
quote.text: Wrex: I need to get my blood flowing. Find me something to kill!

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To proceed; to issue forth; to emanate.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book VII”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: Those thousand decencies that daily flow / From all her words and actions.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To move or match smoothly, gracefully, or continuously.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “Dedication”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Virgil  […]  is  […] sweet and flowing in his hexameters.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To have or be in abundance; to abound, so as to run or flow over.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Joel 3:18:
quote.text: […]  in that day […]  the hils shall flow with milke […]

quote.citation: 1845, John Wilson, The Genius and Character of Robert Burns:
quote.text: the exhilaration of a night that needed not the influence of the flowing bowl

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To hang loosely and wave.

quote.citation: 1788, Publius [pseudonym; Alexander Hamilton], “Number LXVII”, in The Federalist: A Collection of Essays, Written in Favour of the New Constitution,  […] , volume II, New York, N.Y.:  […]  J. and A. M‘Lean, […], →OCLC, page 222:
quote.text: […] the imperial purple flowing in his train.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To rise, as the tide; opposed to ebb.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Second Part of Henry the Fourth, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iii]:
quote.text: The river hath thrice flowed, no ebb between.

definitions.definition: (transitive, computing) To arrange (text in a wordprocessor, etc.) so that it wraps neatly into a designated space; to reflow.
(transitive) To allow (a liquid) to flow.

quote.citation: 1932, Carl Ernest Reistle, Paraffin and Congealing-Oil Problems, volumes 340-349, page 45:
quote.text: The action is usually progressive, and as a certain amount of oil is flowed from the tubing it lowers the pressure on the remaining oil and liberates more gas, thus causing additional oil to flow from the tubing.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cover with water or other liquid; to overflow; to inundate; to flood.
(transitive) To cover with varnish.
(intransitive) To discharge excessive blood from the uterus.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Uncertain. Perhaps from Old Norse flói (“a large bay, firth”), see floe. Compare Scots flow (“peat-bog, marsh”), Icelandic flói (“marshy ground”).

definitions.definition: (Scotland) A bog or mire, especially a rough, waterlogged one.

quote.citation: 1794, John Sinclair, The Statistical Account of Scotland, volume 10, page 328:
quote.text: […]  there are other extensive mosses in this district, commonly called flowes, which it is not probable ever will, or ever can be, converted into arable land. Some of these flowes are found to be 20, 25, or 30 feet deep, and are, besides, such a dead level, that the water has little or no descent; and even supposing they should be cast, or burnt to the bottom, standing pools of dirty water could only stand in their place.
Ye'll stick in some flow, Or, ye'll melt in a thow
Had been roughly laid with bog-wood dug from the flowes,
Dandering o'er ferney knowes, [...] Springing o'er bogs an' flowes, [...]

quote.citation: 1898 July 23, Shetland News, quoted in the EDD:
quote.text: If dey wirna a day apo' da flow dan he [it] wis nae man's bishaness.
